item.title: Brazil’s Most Divided Town Shows the Nation’s Shift to the Right
item.description:
It felt like doomsday for the Brazilian left. On Oct. 4, Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing presidential candidate, outperformed polls and edged ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist.

The narrow margin was not enough to avoid a runoff on Sunday between the two candidates, but it was plenty to set off hand-wringing and soul-searching across progressive bubbles in big cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and a reorganization in Mr. Lula’s campaign.

A visit to Nanuque, a cattle-raising, churchgoing town 500 miles north of Rio de Janeiro, where crowds turn out on foot for an annual march for Jesus and on horseback for the nation’s independence day, offers clues to Mr. Lula’s lackluster showing and Mr. Bolsonaro’s rise.

The town of 35,000 sits in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, which has backed the winner in every presidential election since 1988, when democracy returned to Brazil after a military dictatorship.

Atlantic

Ocean

Amazon R.

BRAZIL

MINAS GERAIS

BOLIVIA

Nanuque

São Paulo

Rio de Janeiro

ARGENTINA

500 miles

The New York Times

In the 2022 race, Nanuque, pronounced nah-NEW-key, was the most closely divided of Brazil’s 5,569 municipalities, with Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, winning by one vote. (Jair Bolsonaro lost that election to Mr. Lula and was convicted of plotting a coup after trying to hold onto power.)

In 2026’s first round, the younger Bolsonaro finished ahead by two percentage points, the same margin he claimed in Brazil as a whole.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s ability to win similar towns — rooted in agriculture and with a strong Evangelical Christian presence — contributed to his strong first round showing.

He won 79 percent of towns with a large agricultural sector, a high percentage of evangelical Christians and that have less than 50,000 residents, according to an analysis by Marco Faganello, a political data scientist at Fundação Getulio Vargas, a Brazilian university. Jair Bolsonaro won 53 percent of such towns in 2022’s first round.

In interviews with scores of voters in Nanuque, including truck drivers, cattle ranchers, farmworkers, business leaders and civil servants, those who have abandoned Mr. Lula cited unfulfilled economic promises, his past corruption scandals and their frustration with health care, among other reasons.

While many on the left remain staunch supporters of Mr. Lula, others who had voted for him before expressed fatigue over an 80-year-old incumbent running for a fourth term. His Workers’ Party has been in power for 18 of the last 24 years.

Valdirene Santos Moura, a cook who has voted for Mr. Lula before, acknowledged his accomplishments, including introducing programs that helped the poor. But now, she said, she was “tired of him already.”

Geremias Alves de Souza, a coffee picker, dropped his voice so his wife would not hear him say he was voting for Mr. Bolsonaro. He said he associates the younger Mr. Bolsonaro with his father’s tough on crime policies.

Other voters said their support for Mr. Bolsonaro was based not on his track record — which they said they were unfamiliar with — but on their affection for Jair Bolsonaro.

Some said they were simply fed up with politics and were planning to abstain on Sunday.

One is Jovenildo Carvalho, 45, who runs a start-up that uses drones to deploy wasps to attack caterpillars that ravage sugar cane fields.

Mr. Carvalho, who grew up with no electricity and wore Che Guevara T-shirts in college, said he has no faith in either candidate’s ability to lead the country, and was frustrated by Brazil’s deeply polarized political landscape.

“I’d like to see Brazil without the veil of fanaticism and blind passion that it has today,” he said.

Agribusiness in Brazil, which includes farming, cattle ranching, meatpacking plants and ethanol distilleries, has become a behemoth, accounting for a quarter of the country’s economy. For the first time, Brazil may soon surpass the United States in agricultural exports.

The sector’s leaders are among Mr. Lula’s biggest detractors, criticizing him over high interest rates, environmental regulations and gas subsidies that have reduced ethanol demand during the Iran war.

“If it were Lula against a stray dog, everyone would vote for the stray dog,” said Luiz Daniel Silva Rocha, whose family owns DASA, a large sugar mill and ethanol distillery outside Nanuque that employs hundreds of people.

The biggest target for local business leaders is Mr. Lula’s signature welfare program, known as Bolsa Família, which provides cash transfers to low income families. Brazilians agree that it has helped pull millions out of extreme poverty, but some now consider it a handout to those who aren’t financially desperate.

“In Brazil today, the policy is to reward those who don’t work,” said Ângelo Márcio Sousa Silva, DASA’s general manager.

Nearly 3,000 families in Nanuque receive cash transfers, according to government data, and business leaders say it has made it hard for them to fill jobs. Between DASA and the town’s largest employer, a meatpacking plant, there are about 120 full-time vacancies, leaving the plants operating below capacity.

The Bolsa Família program came up repeatedly as a driving force behind people’s votes for both candidates, far more than topics that dominate election talk among urban elites, like a scandal roiling Brazil’s Supreme Court or worries about U.S. interference in Latin American elections.

People who work in the informal sector — as day laborers on farms or cleaning houses — but still receive cash benefits remain loyal to Mr. Lula.

Letícia Silva de Almeida, 33, is among those. She works seasonally helping harvest coffee and earns $24 per day. She also receives $150 a month through the cash transfer program, even though she said that money was not essential.

“If they cut it off today, I’d be OK,” she said.

That mind-set infuriates others. Tatiane Souza da Silva, a housekeeper, said friends urged her to understate her income to qualify for the cash program, but she has refused on principle.

“I see young women in good health — men too — refusing to work,” she said. “That ends up hurting the economy.” Once a Lula voter, she plans to vote for Mr. Bolsonaro on Sunday.

Mr. Lula has called Brazil’s free public health system “one of the masterpieces of health care worldwide.’’

That is not a word many in Nanuque would use. Many complained of long waits for specialists in faraway cities, even though a year ago, Mr. Lula launched a program meant to help underserved towns called “Now There Are Specialists.”

“We need the politicians to see us, when it comes to health care,” said Ana Paula Rodrigues dos Santos, 41, who was shopping for the lunches she cooks and sells for $6 each to make a living.

She said she needs her gall bladder removed but explained that the town’s public hospital lacks an intensive care unit, which her doctors have told her she may need since her obesity increases the risk of complications.

She has been on a waiting list at a hospital in a city three hours away for nearly three years, she said.

Ms. dos Santos described herself as an independent who was leaning toward Mr. Bolsonaro.

“It’s been going left, left, left and the left didn’t do anything for Brazil,” she said. “We have to put in new people.”

The right’s increased appeal among voters is not just fueled by growing frustration with Mr. Lula. It is also driven by religion. The percentage of Brazil’s population that is evangelical Christian has tripled since 1991, and members of Evangelical congregations lean heavily conservative.

Dozens of Evangelical churches dot rich and poor neighborhoods in Nanuque, where some pastors preach opposition to abortion and homosexuality.

At New Life Evangelical Church, a relatively wealthy congregation, the pastor, Bishop Robson Merry Teixeira Farias, said he believed nearly all of his 300 members would support Mr. Bolsonaro for president.

Even within less well off congregations, support for Mr. Bolsonaro was still strong, according to pastors and members.

Under Brazilian law, religious leaders cannot make endorsements from the pulpit, but Bishop Merry, as he is known, suggested that preferences can be telegraphed by promoting conservative values that align with specific candidates.

“We do not champion men, we champion causes,” he said.

In a town with no mall or cinema, churches are central to social life, and congregants arrive well dressed and as eager to socialize as to pray.

On Sunday, after church services, they will have a second chance to socialize — at Nanuque’s 21 polling stations.

“As the election approaches, it is the responsibility of leaders” like him, Bishop Merry said, “to pass along their vision.”

“The sheep always try to imitate the pastor,” he added.

Silvia Ribeiro contributed reporting from Rio de Janeiro.

item.title: Why El Salvador’s Strongman Is Directing Threats at Haitian Gangs
item.description:
The skies above the slums and hills of Port-au-Prince are buzzing with helicopters.

Some of them are manned by a team of Salvadoran soldiers, medics and technicians who fly with machine guns at the ready in case they are fired upon.

The Salvadorans are deployed to Haiti as part of an international mission called the Gang Suppression Force aimed at eradicating rampant gang violence. Often tasked with evacuating the injured and transporting soldiers over gang territory, the Salvadorans once flew across the country to pick up a Sri Lankan soldier who had broken his legs.

The Salvadoran contingent in the U.N.-backed force is now the focal point of a high-stakes rescue operation after four of its members were ambushed on Sunday and went missing. Hundreds of Salvadoran special forces are expected to arrive in Haiti in the coming days, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

The episode marks a critical flashpoint in the Gang Suppression Force’s deployment, quickly escalating what critics worried was a slow, underwhelming start to the mission. With El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, warning of a severe military response if his soldiers are not returned alive, the U.N.-backed mission threatens to become a showdown between Haiti’s armed groups and El Salvador’s contentious leader.

For the first time, the understaffed Gang Suppression Force, known as the G.S.F., is conducting operations in Croix-des-Bouquets, a town outside the capital where the Salvadorans were abducted that is one of the country’s most entrenched gang strongholds.

“I think this is a wake up call,” said Louis-Henri Mars, senior adviser of the Institute for Research and Action for Peace, a peace-building organization in Port-au-Prince, the capital. “Wake up call for the international community, for the U.S., for everybody: ‘Hey, we’ve been fooling around here, and those guys are not fooling around. Let’s get it on.’”

The New York Times spent three days last month with the international force, including with the Salvadoran helicopter unit. Troops from a Chadian contingent conducted patrols in armored personnel carriers. The commander of the international mission is from Mongolia.

But the force has been dogged by late deployments and logistics problems, which experts say have led gangs to meet the mission’s arrival with a collective shrug.

Haiti’s gangs control many parts of Port-au-Prince, forcing residents to flee some neighborhoods that have become no man’s lands. In others, gangs are so entrenched that even the police do not dare enter.

More than 22,000 people have been killed in a spiral of gang violence that worsened since the assassination of Haiti’s president five years ago — more than 5,000 so far this year alone. Gangs, once controlled by powerful elites and politicians, outgrew their overseers and banded together, taking over major roads and entire communities.

Touring a former school that the G.S.F. had cleared of gangs, Maj. Tahir Bahar, of Chad, acknowledged that his troops faced a steep learning curve: They’re used to deserts, not cramped urban terrain.

Expectations from Haitians are high, but he promised improvements.

“They want results,” Maj. Bahar said. “We must do it. I cannot promise a timeline.”

Haiti’s ability to hold cleared areas remains a critical obstacle for long-term results, including elections that had been scheduled for December that many here consider an extremely unrealistic goal. The school, in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, is an area so dangerous that it still lacks residents and basic services.

“We need someone to come in after us,” Maj. Bahar said. “The civilians want to come back. They need electricity, and they need schools. We cannot bring electricity.”

The G.S.F. arrived in April with a mandate to take the fight to the gangs and take back control. Unlike a previous international initiative known as the Multinational Security Support mission, it would be five times larger, conduct intelligence-led operations, have arrest powers and work independently without having to coordinate with the Haitian National Police.

It is also funded by contributions to a dedicated U.N. trust fund. Expected to cost about $400 million a year, the fund has received $194 million, according to U.N. records.

The mission is supposed to have 5,500 soldiers, with contributions from countries around the world. Six months later, it only recently reached 2,000 troops, from six nations.

Troop contributions have been delayed, and moving people, vehicles and equipment across the world has proved a challenge.

The international force has cleared gang roadblocks, seized weapons and regularly conducts patrols in downtown Port-au-Prince, freeing up the Haitian National Police to respond to serious outbreaks of violence.

But of 26 arrests the force has made since its arrival, 18 people were released for lack of evidence. In one city, Gros-Morne, gangs killed civilians in retaliation for G.S.F. operations.

“We’ve got a long way to go, we totally recognize that,” Jack Christofides, the force’s special representative, said in an interview last month. “I don’t believe the gangs can sustain a fight against professional soldiers coming from so many different countries. We’ve got real capabilities coming — not just infantry, but police, we’ve got a maritime unit, we’ve got an air unit.”

The mission should have most of its forces on the ground by the end of this year and be making more progress by early next year, he said.

“We’re not saying that in two years’ time there will be no gangs in Haiti,” he said. “What we’re saying is that in two years’ time the Haitian state will no longer need an international force such as ours, because they can look after their own security and eventually stabilize the situation.”

From his social media posts, it does not appear that President Bukele plans to wait that long. In a message written in Creole directed to the Haitian gang members who abducted the four Salvadorans, he warned military operations would only get more intense.

“We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he wrote.

Mr. Bukele, in office since 2019, is both praised and criticized for a harsh crack down on Salvadoran gangs that put tens of thousands of people in prison. El Salvador used to be one of the world’s most dangerous countries; now it’s among the safest.

The Salvadoran technicians went missing on Sunday after coming under attack while driving back from a supermarket through a gang-controlled area. Their vehicle was discovered burned, but the four Salvadorans have not been heard from since.

Although the attention is focused on finding them, the episode has raised serious questions about what they were doing driving through what is widely considered a “no-go” zone for foreigners and even most Haitians. While the incident is being treated as a kidnapping, many experts fear the men have been executed.

On Thursday, Lanmò Sanjou, a gang leader in the area where the Salvadorans were taken, released a video in which he refers to Mr. Bukele and shows buckets full of bullets.

“We will fight to stay alive,” he said.

Gédéon Jean, the director of the Center for Human Rights Analysis and Research in Port-au-Prince, said Haiti needed an international force to help shore up the local police, but that requires adequate technological and human resources.

“Unfortunately, this is still not the case, although the efforts are commendable,” Mr. Jean said. “We are still waiting for a full and complete deployment, and especially for tangible results.”

The ambush of the four Salvadorans will be a turning point for the international mission, he said.

“The disappearance of the four Salvadorans changes the situation,” he said, “because now it is the G.S.F. that is the victim of gang violence.”

André Paultre and Michael Anthony Adams contributed reporting.

item.title: Could Latin America’s Most Famous Leftist Be on the Brink of Defeat?
item.description:
No politician has made a bigger mark on Brazil than President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Over three terms in office, he helped lift millions out of poverty, fought for workers’ rights and became, for a time, the face of a powerful leftist tide sweeping Latin America.

But the political currents have changed drastically and Mr. Lula, the region’s most influential statesman, is now facing a tough battle as he seeks another term. If he is defeated on Sunday, as polls suggest he might be, it would be the biggest win yet for the right-wing surge barreling through Latin America.

Right-wing candidates, aligned with President Trump on fighting drug gangs and waging culture wars, have won seven straight Latin American elections in the past 18 months.

As the region’s largest country, Brazil represents a major prize. A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would tighten the right’s claim on Latin America, leaving Mexico the last big country controlled by the left.

Mr. Lula has offered a rare example of resistance to Washington’s strategy to project military and economic might in the region, pushing back against Mr. Trump as he has tried to squeeze Brazil with tariffs and sanctions.

By contrast, Mr. Lula’s right-wing opponent, Mr. Bolsonaro, has promised to join a U.S.-led regional security alliance and has offered Brazil’s vast critical mineral deposits as a way to lessen American reliance on China.

Mr. Lula, 80, is heading into Sunday’s race as the underdog, having drawn fewer voters than Mr. Bolsonaro in a first round of elections this month. Yet the margin between the two leading candidates was the smallest in Brazil’s history, with polls suggesting a narrowing race for the presidency.

In the final stretch of campaigning, Mr. Lula and his allies have worked to mobilize millions of Brazilians, on social media and on the streets.

Mr. Lula has also challenged Mr. Bolsonaro to open up his financial statements and phone records to public scrutiny, vowing to do the same. Mr. Bolsonaro has said he will oblige only after reviewing Mr. Lula’s records, which the leftist offered to electoral authorities this week.

What has become clear is that Mr. Bolsonaro’s promises to tackle organized crime, high grocery bills and a sluggish economy have resonated with millions of working-class Brazilians who in the past may have cast a ballot for Mr. Lula.

“It’s really about this profound sense of fatigue,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies the rise of the Brazilian right, said of Mr. Lula. “It’s the feeling that this leader, this project, has already run its course — alongside a deep desire for renewal.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Lula has pointed to his economic achievements over the last four years, while also warning that restoring the Bolsonaro family to power poses a risk to Brazil’s democracy. Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year-sentence for attempting a coup after losing the last election to Mr. Lula.

Mr. Lula has also defended his broader political legacy, built on decades of social programs that relieved widespread hunger, expanded education opportunities and reduced deep inequality in the last nation in the Americas to abolish slavery.

“Inequality and underdevelopment are the result of policy choices,” Mr. Lula told the United Nations General Assembly in September. “It is possible to include the poor in the budget and make the rich pay their fair share.”

Yet the leftist leader, whom former President Barack Obama once called the “most popular politician on Earth,” has struggled to stir excitement among Brazilian voters whose electoral priorities appear to have shifted.

Even though in the past four years Brazil’s economy has grown modestly and unemployment has fallen to its lowest rates on record, rising household debt and an affordability crisis have left many ordinary Brazilians feeling worse off.

Some of Mr. Bolsonaro’s libertarian ideas, like a hands-off state, lower taxes and cutting red tape for the self-employed, have also appealed to a growing portion of the working class that is migrating to the gig economy.

“There is a new kind of working class in Brazil,” said Rosana Pinheiro-Machado, a professor at University College Dublin who studies Brazil’s populist movements. “And it has a new way of viewing prosperity.”

If Mr. Lula is to secure a victory on Sunday, he will have to win over some of the millions of Brazilians who in the first round stayed home, voted for other losing candidates or annulled their ballots.

In an effort to lift his approval rating heading into the elections, Mr. Lula has increased how much people receive under the government’s signature welfare program and granted temporary fuel subsidies to ease the pain of rising prices because of the war in Iran.

He also expanded a government program to relieve indebted Brazilians facing billions of dollars in consumer loans. And just days before the first round of voting, he banned online betting, which has accelerated Brazil’s spiraling personal debt crisis.

This is not the first time Mr. Lula faces an uphill climb. Less than a decade ago, he was sitting in a prison cell, serving a 12-year sentence over a corruption scandal that appeared to have ended his political career.

But his convictions were annulled by the Supreme Court in 2021 amid evidence that the judge, prosecutors and the police had colluded to put him behind bars. This freed Mr. Lula to run against the elder Mr. Bolsonaro in 2022, a race he won in a huge political comeback.

Mr. Lula emerged on the political stage in the 1970s, making his name as a union leader on the outskirts of São Paulo. As president between 2003 and 2010, Mr. Lula, a former metalworker with a fifth-grade education, created generous social programs that helped some 20 million Brazilians climb out of poverty.

On the world stage, he has elevated Brazil to a leader on issues such as poverty, hunger and climate change, in part through his efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest. A skilled diplomat, Mr. Lula has also cemented Brazil’s reputation abroad as an important emerging power in the Global South.

When he left office in 2010, Mr. Lula’s approval ratings topped 80 percent. But the scandal that landed him in prison tarnished his reputation with a large slice of Brazil’s population, who still link him and his political party to corruption. Even after returning to the presidency, Mr. Lula has struggled to regain the trust of many voters.

Now, a new corruption scandal embroiling much of Brazil’s political and judicial elite, including Mr. Bolsonaro himself, is adding to the fatigue many Brazilians feel toward their political leaders. With the crisis unfolding on Mr. Lula’s watch, it has further dampened enthusiasm around his candidacy.

Ultimately, Brazilians will have to decide whether they still share his vision for Brazil’s future.

And, even if Mr. Lula is able to secure another victory, he will face the daunting task of governing a bitterly divided nation and navigating a legislative branch that has swung sharply to the right.

“Even if President Lula wins,” said Ms. Rocha, the political scientist, “it still marks, in a sense, the decline of a certain kind of leftism, of his Workers’ Party, and of Lula himself.”

item.title: Paris, Battened Down Against Riots, Offers Lonely Welcome to Visitors
item.description:
A locked-down Paris is a headache for locals. But it was a heartache on Saturday for first-time visitors from Louisiana, who traveled here for an N.F.L. football game between the New Orleans Saints and Pittsburgh Steelers and found the Louvre museum closed and the Arc de Triomphe ringed by police vans.

“Just about everything is closed,” said Terri Wallis, 65, a school principal and Saints fan from Baton Rouge, who was visiting with three generations of her family. “You know, we’re not wealthy people. This is a once-in-a-lifetime trip to come and see the Mona Lisa. So, this is a little disappointing.”

The French authorities deployed as many as 70,000 police officers and gendarmes to prevent a repeat of last weekend, when mass protests degenerated into arson, looting and other violence. Officials in Paris and other cities hard hit by the unrest enforced curfews and temporary restrictions on gatherings.

In Paris, fears of another outbreak of violence prompted several cultural institutions, including the Louvre, Grand Palais, Orsay, Orangerie and Picasso museums, to close.

Ms. Wallis and her family were kicking around in a food store on the Avenue des Champs-Élysées, the city’s grandest boulevard, where traffic was light and private security guards were posted at most businesses’ entrances. All along the street, shops and boutiques were boarded up to protect them from looters.

With major cultural sites closed, Paris felt less chaotic than battened-down on a slate-gray Saturday afternoon. At the Louvre, a chain stretched across the door at the museum’s pyramid entrance. The Tuileries Gardens were also closed — because of high winds, a sign said.

While Notre-Dame Cathedral was open, Ms. Wallis said the lines outside it were extremely long, as tourists flocked to one of their few remaining options.

A midday bicycle ride through Paris revealed an eerily empty city. The Place de la Bastille, famous as the site of uprisings during the French Revolution and more recently the locus for student-led protests, had been ruled off-limits to demonstrators by the Paris authorities on Saturday.

A police phalanx, backed by a water-cannon truck and officers on motorcycles, kept the square clear. The police warned over a loudspeaker that anyone who tried to organize an illegal protest would be fined 135 euros, about $150.

“It’s not possible to stay here regardless of why you are here,” the voice on the loudspeaker said. “I ask you to leave the square.”

The authorities pushed the protesters to the southern periphery of the city, a last-minute change in the approved route for the march, which the organizers said was calculated to sow disarray in their ranks. Whether it would avert a repeat of the arson and looting that broke out across Paris last weekend was not yet clear.

Ms. Wallis said she considered calling off the trip after seeing those riots. But the Saints-Steelers game, the first N.F.L. match ever played in Paris, will go ahead as scheduled on Sunday in the Stade de France, a stadium in the Paris suburbs a few miles from where the high school protest movement began last month.

In those demonstrations, students erected barricades in front of their schools to protest dilapidated buildings, a shortage of teachers and a university admissions process that many say is opaque and unfair.

Chelsea Bertrand, who was with the Wallis family and works at an elementary school in Baton Rouge, said that as an educator, she was impressed by how the French students had mobilized, even if it affected her visit.

“You teach them to speak up for what’s right,” she said. “The fact that they’re actually standing up in a positive way — how it originally started — for their rights and what they think is best for education — I think that’s amazing.”

The women said they hadn’t witnessed any unrest and weren’t worried about their safety. Ms. Wallis said marveled at how “nonchalant” some people appeared to be about the disorder, pointing to a viral video on social media that appeared to show a couple relaxing in a cafe last weekend while fires burned outside.

“I thought, ‘OK, that’s the French,’” Ms. Wallis said. “The city’s burning and y’all are just sitting there.”

item.title: What’s at Stake in Brazil’s Elections?
item.description:
A number of right-wing leaders have recently swept into power in Latin America, riding a wave of dissatisfaction with incumbent governments and deepening worries about security and a rising cost of living.

Until now, Brazil, the region’s largest nation, had been the exception. The left-wing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, began his third nonconsecutive term in 2023. His predecessor and rival, Jair Bolsonaro, had been convicted of trying to stage a coup to prevent Mr. Lula from taking office and was sentenced to 27 years, which he is currently serving under house arrest for health reasons.

Now Mr. Lula, weighed down by widespread perceptions of rising crime and economic woes, faces a challenge from the former president’s son, Flávio Bolsonaro, a right-wing senator. Mr. Bolsonaro’s formidable performance in the first voting round this month gave him the edge going into a two-way contest.

The outcome will have a profound effect on Brazil and its relations with the United States in particular. Here are some of the major issues at stake.

Mr. Bolsonaro has already said he would add Brazil to the Trump administration’s anti-cartel coalition, called the Shield of the Americas, and work with the United States to fight Brazilian gangs.

He suggested in social media posts last year that he would welcome U.S. military intervention in Brazil, though he denied that in recent interviews, saying the cooperation would be limited to intelligence. But it was Mr. Bolsonaro who successfully lobbied Mr. Trump to designate two Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups.

Mr. Lula has resisted joining the coalition, warning that intertwining too closely with the United States on security matters could threaten the nation’s sovereignty.

The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazilian products in an unsuccessful pressure campaign to disrupt the prosecution of Jair Bolsonaro. Many of those tariffs were eventually scaled back, and Brazil’s economy has remained largely unharmed by President Trump’s tariff campaign.

Another term for Mr. Lula, however, would increase the risk of more economic conflicts with the United States that might hurt the Brazilian economy. Of course, Mr. Bolsonaro would not be immune to those problems; Mr. Trump has been known to levy tariffs against allies as well as adversaries.

The Trump administration has signaled an interest in importing Brazilian oil to counter disruptions related to the Iran war and the country’s rare-earth minerals to reduce U.S. dependence on China for those resources. Mr. Bolsonaro is expected to align Brazil more closely with the United States than Mr. Lula has on trade issues, but neither leader can afford to anger China, a major trading partner.

The election could also affect Brazil’s ability to negotiate trade with the United States as a bloc with other countries in the region.

“Brazil’s relations with its neighbors have been extremely challenging,” said Carolina Moehlecke, an assistant professor of international relations at Getúlio Vargas Foundation, a research institution. This was especially true of its neighbor, Argentina, she added, whose right-wing president is a close ally of Mr. Trump. Mr. Bolsonaro, she said, might have an easier time cooperating with fellow right-wing leaders in Latin America.

If Mr. Bolsonaro carries the vote, conservationists fear a return to his father’s policies of allowing rapid deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, a trend that was largely reversed under President Lula. The younger Mr. Bolsonaro does not believe that climate change is caused by humans and has defended opening up protected lands to mining and farming.

He has also pledged to stem the nation’s rising debt. If he attempts to accomplish that through cuts to public spending, that could prove politically sensitive, Ms. Moehlecke said, especially when it comes to social welfare policies with broad popularity in Brazil. In the lead-up to Sunday’s elections, Mr. Lula had promised to increase welfare payments.

Mr. Lula has framed the election as a test of the nation’s democracy and portrays the Bolsonaros as a threat to democratic institutions. Ms. Moehlecke said it was likely Mr. Bolsonaro would take the country in a more authoritarian direction, though his rhetoric is generally tamer than his father’s.

But if Mr. Bolsonaro wins, his party’s gains in the legislature could allow him to deliver on some of his most polarizing promises: amnesty for his father, pardons for rioters who stormed Brazil’s halls of power after the last election, and a Senate more willing to try to remove justices who convicted his father.

If Mr. Lula wins, he most likely will face significant checks against his power. Right-wing candidates, including four other members of the Bolsonaro family, have made significant strides in the nation’s legislative races.

item.title: Modi’s Plan to Stop India’s Protests
item.description:
It’s been quite something to watch India’s student protests, which started this summer and have continued, off and on, into the fall. So far, they’ve forced the resignation of a minister and put Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the back foot — a rare occurrence.

It’s tempting to compare these demonstrations to the youth protests currently roiling Europe. But there’s at least one important difference: Young people make up a much larger share of India’s population than they do in Europe — which is one reason these protests have been so powerful. (When I read about them, my mind actually went to the student protests of 1968, which took place when the West itself had a youth bulge and which ended up reshaping Western societies profoundly.)

Today, I write about why the youth movement has Modi nervous — and whom he’d rather face off against instead.

This time, Modi was prepared.

As India braced for another round of Gen Z protests in New Delhi this month, the government swiftly barricaded a large area of the city center and deployed tens of thousands of security forces to stop crowds like those that had gathered during the summer from mobilizing.

But as my colleagues Mujib Mashal, Suhasini Raj and Hari Kumar reported, the police did allow one large gathering to go ahead: the one staged by the Congress Party and its alliance partners. Led by India’s opposition leader, Rahul Gandhi, they were able to march to the Supreme Court, where they raged against the prime minister’s strongman tactics and efforts to chip away at India’s democracy by removing millions of names from voter rolls.

Why would Modi’s government go to such enormous lengths to crack down on protests by a youth movement but let one by the opposition go forward? It might seem like a puzzle, until you appreciate — as Mujib points out — that it’s part of a strategy that Modi has adopted in the aftermath of this summer’s protests.

Modi is deliberately trying to make the ongoing demonstrations less about the youth movement that unleashed them, and more about his traditional opposition.

Because that’s a fight he knows how to win.

The devil you know

When young people first took to the streets this summer to protest against a botched university entrance exam and an education system they said was failing them, the government was caught by surprise.

Modi tried to contain the protests, first with police batons and tear gas, then with social media videos trying to connect with Gen Z, in its own style. It didn’t work. In the end, he had to sacrifice his education minister.

It was a rare political climb-down for a leader who has been in power for 12 years. The protesters went home, for a while at least. But, as Mujib writes, they were also emboldened.

India’s youth movement is a headache for Modi, and he’s been struggling to find a workable playbook. Partly that’s because India has a lot of young people: more than 40 percent of India’s 1.4 billion people are under 25. And partly it’s because the youth movement has cut across traditional political divides in India, making it much harder for Modi and his allies to box in and demonize.

It’s no coincidence that this movement first galvanized around the issue of dysfunction in India’s higher education system — specifically, leaked entrance-exam questions, Mujib told me. The sense that access to the university system is rigged — a system that Indians have long been told is their ticket to a better life — cuts across typical political lines.

“The anger was over an issue that couldn’t easily be dismissed as partisan,” Mujib said. This, for Modi, is something new. One detail that stood out to me: Many of the young protesters this summer said they came from middle-class families that support Modi’s party, the B.J.P.

The Congress Party, by contrast, is very much a known quantity. Modi has never lost an election against a rival from the Congress Party. His party beat Congress three times in national elections. And the man leading the losing side was always the same — Gandhi, who is still in charge today.

Mujib interviewed more than half a dozen senior members of Modi’s coalition to talk about the B.J.P.’s strategy in the face of these protests.

Modi’s approach is two-pronged, Mujib explains: First, quash any protests that could feel like a continuation of the Gen Z protests over the summer, which, by all accounts, unsettled his grip on power.

And second, allow the rallies of traditional opposition parties to go ahead, framing the fight squarely against a foe that Modi has repeatedly beaten at elections and is confident of beating again.

So far, Mujib writes, it seems to be working. Efforts to detain the leaders of the cockroach movement have slowed its momentum; meanwhile, Congress is planning its own rally for Nov. 1.

Common cause?

What happens next will depend in part on the extent to which Modi continues pursuing his crackdown. But it might also depend on whether Gandhi and the youth movement want to stand together.

For Gandhi, it’s potentially an opportunity. His longtime campaign against Modi’s strongman tactics has been validated and energized by this year’s protests. Images of him using his legs to push back against police officers trying to shove him inside a bus earlier this month went viral on social media, my colleague Anupreeta Das reported. So did a video of him climbing up a yellow police barricade to avoid being captured by security forces.

During the march to the Supreme Court earlier this month, he was joined by Neha Bora, a student who has become a breakout star of the youth protests.

In a sense, Gandhi is trying to do precisely what Modi wants him to do: weave the youth protests and political opposition into a unified force.

The question is whether such an alliance would undermine the power of the youth movement, which is in part rooted in its nonpartisan appeal.

Whatever happens, India’s youth movement has become a serious factor in Indian politics. Gandhi is hoping it will galvanize his political ambitions. And Modi is under pressure in a way he has not been in his 12 years at the national helm.

Brazilians cast their ballots yesterday in a fiercely fought presidential election that has the country on edge.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist who has repeatedly defied Trump, is facing a challenge from Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is aligned with Washington on issues such as using lethal force to fight drug gangs. Follow our live coverage.

My colleague Ana Ionova explains in the video above how Bolsonaro has focused his campaign message on fighting crime, a strategy from the right-wing playbook in other Latin American countries.

Venezuela’s leading opposition leader, María Corina Machado, returned to her country after nearly a year in exile. Read our recent interview with her.

Weekend protests in France ended with clashes but did not escalate into widespread looting.

Saudi Arabia reopened the Riyadh airport after a spate of deadly Houthi attacks.

The war in Iran is entering a dangerous phase ahead of elections in the U.S. and Israel.

The Israeli military raided Hebron, in the West Bank, after an attack killed two soldiers.

North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, visited China for the first time in more than a year.

Barack Obama sharply criticized Trump during appearances on the campaign trail.

Americans in their 30s say the cost of living is keeping them from milestones like buying a house or starting a family. It’s affecting how they vote.

Airbnb said it would restrict the chores required of guests after complaints from travelers.

The owners of Elvis Presley’s music sued Anthropic, saying it trained its A.I. models on more than 200 of Presley’s songs without permission.

The most clicked link in your newsletter on Friday was about an Emily Dickinson poem.

The slogan has appeared on protest signs in France. It means “In the name of God, it’s the darkness,” which doesn’t make much sense. But it has become a rallying cry. Some suspect that the phrase was a clumsy attempt by the authorities to infiltrate the student movements.

Cheese nerds are an excitable bunch. These days, if you want to see them get superexcited, just mention Canada.

Canadian cheesemakers have been winning awards, with one even running an organic operation in which cows rest on water beds after grazing. But the 50 percent tariffs that Trump imposed on Canadian cheese last month have caused havoc. Read more about how tariffs are affecting cheese.

In 2014, Kelly Green made a decision that would change her life: She moved to Tristan da Cunha, a remote island in the South Atlantic. Two years before, she had met an islander on a visit to the British overseas territory.

She married him, and she’s now raising a family in the quiet outpost, where they grow potatoes and raise sheep. Only 220 people live on the island, which she reached after leaving South Africa and spending a week at sea. “Raising a family here is amazing,” Green said. Read more about life on Tristan.

Discover: A road trip through Lithuania and Latvia turns up extraordinary country inns.

Watch: The underdog love story “Wicker” argues that even the most reviled among us deserve passion.

This roast chicken recipe calls for 40 cloves of garlic — yes, 40. They are key to making a rich, garlic-infused butter sauce to pour over the chicken and a jammy garlic spread to slather on crusty bread.

item.title: Who Is María Corina Machado?
item.description:
María Corina Machado, the leader of the biggest opposition movement in Venezuela, returned to her country on Sunday after nearly a year in exile since slipping out to receive the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize.

A conservative former lawmaker and a longtime opponent of Venezuela’s socialist ruling party, Ms. Machado has returned to press for elections in a country reeling from the political changes that have taken place since she left and from devastating earthquakes in June.

Just weeks after she traveled to Norway in December to receive the peace prize, the United States in January invaded Venezuela, captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, and backed Delcy Rodríguez, who had been appointed his vice president after a 2024 election widely seen as rigged.

Ms. Machado had been in hiding domestically since Mr. Maduro claimed victory in that election and had to travel abroad secretly. But Mr. Maduro’s removal did not guarantee her return.

Ms. Machado praised the U.S. invasion and gave her Nobel medal to President Trump. While in exile, she pledged to go back and push for elections, including in a recent interview with The New York Times. But until Sunday, her efforts to return were repeatedly thwarted.

“I am here,” Ms. Machado wrote in a message on social media from Venezuela on Sunday. “With you all.”

Here’s what to know about Ms. Machado, the movement she leads and what her return means for Venezuela.

Ms. Machado, 59, is the eldest daughter of a prominent family in Caracas. She attended an elite Catholic girls’ school in Caracas and a boarding school in Wellesley, Mass. She studied engineering and finance, and later worked for the family company, Sivensa, a large steel producer.

Parts of the company were expropriated in 2010 by President Hugo Chávez, the founder of the country’s modern socialist movement, who took control of dozens of privately owned companies as part of his nationalization program.

In the early 2000s, she became a political activist and a founder of Súmate, a voting rights group that led a failed effort to recall Mr. Chávez, who died in 2013.

Mr. Maduro held power in the years that followed until he and his wife, Cilia Flores, were captured in January by the United States, where they both await trial on charges of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and torture of detainees amid violent repression of the political opposition.

Ms. Machado joined the National Assembly in 2010, winning a record number of votes. She leads the Vente Venezuela opposition party and in 2023 announced a bid for the presidency.

But she was blocked from running in the 2024 election because of what the government said were financial irregularities when she was a national legislator. She called this a politically motivated maneuver meant to keep her from power and backed a surrogate, a little-known former diplomat named Edmundo González.

Mr. González ran against Mr. Maduro, who claimed victory in the election.

The opposition, however, collected evidence that it said showed Mr. González won by a wide margin and alleged that Mr. Maduro had stolen the vote. The Carter Center, an independent vote monitoring organization, has called the opposition’s count accurate.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee said last year that it had recognized Ms. Machado primarily for her efforts to advance democracy “in the face of ever-expanding authoritarianism in Venezuela.”

In a statement on Sunday, Ms. Machado’s spokesman, David Smolansky, called her return “a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair and verifiable presidential elections in the near future.”

Ms. Machado was a strong supporter of Mr. Trump’s military buildup in the Caribbean last year. Like Mr. Trump, she argued that Mr. Maduro posed a regional security threat.

In statements to the press before his capture, Ms. Machado said that her movement was prepared to take territorial and administrative control of Venezuela if Mr. Maduro were to fall from power.

She had also promoted an economic plan to American and other investors, saying that a democratic Venezuela under her movement’s control could generate $1.7 trillion in wealth in 15 years, in part by privatizing the oil industry.

The Trump administration seemed to agree with that assessment. Since capturing Mr. Maduro, the United States has moved to privatize the Venezuelan oil industry, allowing Ms. Rodríguez to make opaque financial deals. Ms. Machado recently criticized one of these agreements but has said that she would respect deals that comply with Venezuelan law should she be in power someday.

Ms. Machado gave her Nobel medal to Mr. Trump in a meeting in January, though the peace prize which he has long coveted is not transferable, according to the committee that awards it.

Still, the Trump administration has kept Ms. Machado at a distance.

The relationship between Ms. Machado and the Trump administration grew tense after devastating twin earthquakes struck Venezuela in June, when she pressed for help in returning home and was told there were fears this would destabilize the country.

After the announcement of her return, Mr. Trump told reporters in Washington on Sunday that Ms. Machado is “a very nice woman,” without signaling support for her leadership. “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman,” he said. “But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post on Sunday that “the conditions allowing for the safe return of Ms. Machado is the direct result” of reconciliation efforts in Venezuela that the United States has supported. The post offered no timeline for elections.

“The United States expects the freedoms of all sectors of Venezuelan politics to continue to be respected,” he wrote. “Likewise, we expect all political actors to support these talks which represent the best chance Venezuela has had in thirty years to peacefully achieve not just a free and fair election but an enduring democracy.”

Mr. Smolansky, the aide to Ms. Machado, on Sunday thanked Mr. Trump, Mr. Rubio, the U.S. government, Congress and allied governments for their “continued leadership and support” in his statement about her return.

item.title: Speed of Starshield Satellite Network Is Improving, Ukraine Says
item.description:
Ukrainian drones connected to the Pentagon-funded Starshield satellite network have flown at speeds near 250 miles an hour for the first time since the system was throttled last week, Ukraine’s defense minister announced on Saturday. It was the first sign that the speed restrictions, which have hampered crucial drone operations, might be easing.

“This is another example when direct dialogue and the persistent position of the president of Ukraine at the highest level produce results,” Yevhen Khmara, the defense minister, said in a statement. “And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

Ukraine uses Starshield for air defense and to guide drones toward targets in Russian-occupied territory. The unexplained throttling of the system deepened a growing rift that has been playing out publicly between Ukraine and the United States. President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Ukrainian civilians had been left more vulnerable to Russian attack, and Ukrainian officials raised fears that the Starshield program had been slowed to force Ukraine into capitulation.

Ukrainian drone operators first saw their drones slowed to speeds lower than 40 miles an hour about 10 days ago. Many drones slowed so abruptly that they lost connection to their pilots on the ground and then fell from the sky, wasting expensive equipment.

It remains unclear who, if anyone, ordered the system to be slowed. No one in Washington has taken responsibility, a fact that only caused further confusion in Kyiv.It has also deepened divides between Congress and the White House over the U.S. approach to Russia. A group of Republicans and Democrats in the Senate warned the White House this week that they would block President Trump’s nominations if Ukraine’s full Starshield capabilities were not restored.

item.title: Israel’s High-Stakes Election: What to Know
item.description:
Israelis are heading to the polls on Tuesday to vote in what many say could be one of the most consequential elections in the country’s 78-year history.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, the country’s longest-serving leader, his party and his governing coalition have been locked in a tight contest in the country’s first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault that ignited Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

Every party creates a ranked list of its candidates, and voters choose a party or slate. The leader of the party with the most votes could become the country’s next prime minister — though it is not automatic — if that candidate can form a government, but the parliamentary system is complicated and involves extensive negotiations.

Here’s what to know.

Election Day is a public holiday in Israel, with schools, government offices and many public services closed. In most of the country, polls are scheduled to open at 7 a.m. local time and close at 10 p.m., with hours slightly reduced in some small communities, hospitals and prisons.

Voters are assigned to a polling station near their registered residence and may vote only at that location. There are exceptions for soldiers, people with limited mobility and prisoners, among others.

All Israeli citizens 18 or older who are registered to vote may do so with a valid identification, such as a passport, driver’s license or Israeli identification card. Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the population, could play a significant role in the vote, depending on turnout.

Unlike many democracies, Israel does not have a postal or proxy voting system, and most citizens cannot cast an absentee vote from abroad.

Israel’s electoral system uses nationwide proportional representation. Elections to the Knesset, Israel’s 120-seat Parliament, are held at least every four years, though they can happen more often. In 2022, Israeli elections were held for the fifth time in three years after the Knesset dissolved itself.

Israelis cast a single ballot for a list of candidates affiliated with a party. A party receives a number of seats proportional to the national vote it got. To gain a place in Parliament, however, a party or must receive at least 3.25 percent of the valid votes. About 10 parties are expected to clear that electoral threshold.

Official election results are expected by Nov. 4.

No single party has ever won a majority of votes, which means parties must form factions and party leaders try to forge a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.

Within seven days of the official election results being announced, Israel’s president, who plays a mostly symbolic role, meets with elected representatives of the parliamentary factions.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will assign a member of the Knesset — usually the leader of the party or faction that has won the most seats — to form a government. That candidate then has 28 days to negotiate with other factions and forge alliances to form a government, which must be approved by the Knesset in a vote of confidence. That person can request a 14-day extension to the deadline.

If that effort fails, the president can select another candidate who also has 28 days to try to form a government. If that second attempt fails, a majority of Knesset members can ask the president to have a third candidate try. That person would be granted 14 days to form a government, and if that failed, new elections would be announced

If a candidate who has been selected to form a government can propose one, along with a policy agenda, and their proposal wins a plurality of votes in the Knesset, the government is formally invested, and that candidate becomes the prime minister. Technically, the law allows for a minority government if the relative majority supporting it is larger than the minority opposing, but governments established after elections have almost always enjoyed the confidence of a majority of Knesset members, at least 61.

Historically, it has taken about 20 to 100 days to form a government, and no government has been sworn in less than 50 days after an election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank in Israel.

Different polls in the week ahead of the election have suggested different outcomes, which is “very problematic for political scientists,” said Assaf Shapira, who heads political research at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank in Israel.

Many Israelis consider this election to be a referendum on Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party, and their hard-right allies, are in a close race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who heads the opposition coalition led by the Yashar party and has emerged as Mr. Netanyahu’s top challenger.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Reopens Riyadh Airport After Weeks of Houthi Attacks
item.description:
The authorities in Saudi Arabia reopened an international airport in the capital on Sunday after a spate of deadly attacks, even as the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen vowed to keep striking the facility.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital, said on Saturday night that flights would resume on Sunday. In a statement, it advised travelers to “verify the status of their bookings and flights before heading to the airport.”

The airport had been closed to the public since Oct. 10, when a cruise missile launched by the Houthis struck a passenger terminal, killing at least 13 people and injuring more than 300. The militia, based in northern Yemen, has launched at least three other deadly strikes on the airport this month — part of its near-daily attacks on Riyadh.

On Sunday morning, residents of the capital received an emergency alert warning of an incoming “aerial threat” and some reported hearing several loud booms. The Saudi authorities said soon after that they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh.

A Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, had renewed a warning to airlines and travelers after the airport issued its statement about reopening, saying to avoid using the airport “because it is a military target.” The Saudi government, he said, would “bear responsibility for the consequences” of reopening it.

The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to questions about how they had assessed it was safe to reopen the airport, or if they had put in place additional air defenses.

After four years of relative peace, the Houthis and the Saudis resumed attacking each other earlier this month amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ primary backer.

The Houthis describe their attacks as retaliation for deadly Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, including many that have killed and injured civilians.

On Saturday, Mr. Saree claimed in a statement that the militia had carried out an operation against the airport, among other attacks around the country, without specifying when.

The Saudi authorities have not said whether the airport was targeted this weekend. The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, which is fighting the Houthis, said it had intercepted missiles and drones heading toward Riyadh on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

It was not immediately clear how many flights were departing from or landing in Riyadh airport on Sunday, or whether airlines other than Saudi state-owned carriers would opt to resume flights.

Flightradar24, a flight tracking website, showed that a Saudi Arabian Airlines plane flying from Jeddah had landed in Riyadh on Sunday afternoon. It also showed that dozens of flights to and from Riyadh had been canceled.

In recent weeks, fighting has reignited inside Yemen between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

A Saudi-led bombing campaign launched against the Houthis a decade ago aimed to rout the militia and restore the government. It lasted for years and precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease.

A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace to the country and left the Houthis in control of northern Yemen.

Tensions began to rise again after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, sparking a regional war. In July, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the international airport in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in order to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.

The militia declared a blockade on Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea, and both sides began to launch a series of escalating attacks. After a full-blown war reignited earlier this month, the militia turned its focus to Saudi airports, threatening to turn them into a “theater of military operations.”

In doing so, they have hit at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions to transform the kingdom from an insular, oil-dependent nation into a global hub for business and tourism.

The prince, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, recently launched a new international airline with its hub in Riyadh. His annual investment summit typically draws billionaires, executives and officials from around the world to Riyadh and was set to begin on Monday. However, it was postponed at the last minute until 2027.

The United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said on social media last week.

Despite the Houthi threats, Saudi officials have sought to maintain a sense of normalcy. The authorities kept Riyadh airport open after two deadly attacks, closing it only after the mass casualty event on Oct. 10.

In the face of the attacks, Saudi Arabia has been seeking support from allies. Last week, Britain said that it would send fighter jets to help defend Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from the Houthis.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

item.title: A Day After Renewed Street Clashes in France, Relief and Anxiety Mix
item.description:
For the French government, there was a fleeting sense of relief on Sunday morning as workers in Paris and other cities hauled away charred trash bins and swept up debris after another day of disorder.

Largely peaceful protests on Saturday ended in the evening with clashes between the police and protesters, but as chaotic as the scenes were, they did not escalate into the wholesale arson and looting that engulfed the country a week earlier. A fortified police presence and widespread arrests kept a lid on vandalism, if not preventing it altogether.

Yet the respite could be short-lived. The huge turnout for the demonstrations — 410,000 people nationwide, according to the interior ministry; 800,000, according to the union organizers — suggested that, far from flagging, the protest movement was gaining momentum. Activists called for another day of protests on Oct. 31.

France remains acutely on edge. The killing of a young man in a shooting spree in a suburb of Paris on Friday has only added to the tensions. The authorities have not fully identified the assailant, who was arrested and is currently under psychiatric observation to determine whether his mental health condition is compatible with continuing his interrogations, according to France’s antiterrorism prosecutor’s office.

President Emmanuel Macron of France denounced the shooting as a “racist terrorist attack” and described it as a “turning point” for the country.

French politics, too, may be nearing a fateful transition. On Sunday, Marine Le Pen, the leader of the main far-right party, officially began her campaign to succeed Mr. Macron as president next spring.

“Even if today the words that come to mind are ‘ruin,’ ‘decline,’ ‘oblivion,’ ‘riots,’” Ms. Le Pen told a fired-up crowd of 8,000 supporters on Sunday, “we believe in humanity, in our people, in France and therefore in the future.”

Comparing the current period to the Dark Ages, she vowed to bring about a “Renaissance” — her campaign motto. “I am not proposing to return to the France of before,” she said. “I am proposing to conceive and build the France of tomorrow.”

The unrest has buoyed Ms. Le Pen’s prospects, as she has promised to restore law and order and condemned Mr. Macron for what she says is an ineffectual response. Some 5,000 people applied to become members of her party following the violence on Oct. 17, according to party officials.

“For me, that was the straw that broke the camel’s back,” said Jean-Luc Renaud, 65, a retired tobacco shop owner.

Mr. Renaud drove about six hours from the south of France to support Ms. Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, her protégé and the leader of the party, because “they are the future for a France that truly needs order,” he said.

Other critics accused the government of using heavy-handed tactics to suppress the protests on Saturday. Local authorities refused to allow several rallies and, in Paris, changed the route of the main demonstration at the last minute, so that protesters were pushed from the center of the city to its southeastern periphery.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, blamed the violence on Saturday evening on “ultraleft” activists, repeating a charge the government has made since the unrest began in France’s high schools last month. But there were signs that the government’s argument was wearing thin, especially given the swelling size of the protests, which now include union members, public workers and protesters who were part of the “Yellow Vest” movement, which convulsed France from 2018 to 2020.

Far-left leaders deny they are fomenting the unrest, and they are now joined by skeptical leaders from the center left as well. The Socialist mayors of Paris and Marseille have aimed their criticism not at far-right agitators but at deeper problems that they say are a legacy of Mr. Macron’s nine years in power.

“Events are conspiring to boost Le Pen and distract from her problems and failures,” said Mujtaba Rahman, an analyst who specializes in Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy. He told clients last week that he now expected Ms. Le Pen to win the election, a shift from his view that a centrist candidate would edge her out in the second round of France’s two-round system.

“The centrist candidates are being dragged down by association with Macron,” Mr. Rahman said. While this could change again, he said, “As things stand, everything seems to favor radical change and Le Pen.”

The mood at a two-day congress of Ms. Le Pen’s party, the National Rally, in Orléans, south of Paris, was confident, even jubilant — save for a short-lived attempt by four activists to disrupt Mr. Bardella’s speech. Thomas Aubert, 34, said he had never attended a party event before but felt the need to do something after violence swept through the country. “With everything that’s going on right now, we need to start speaking up a little,” he said.

“We just want safety and we want people to behave themselves,” Mr. Aubert said, adding that he felt the government had not been “firm enough” in its response.

A resident of Orléans who works as an audiovisual project manager, Mr. Aubert said he considered the country’s main problem to be what he described as unbridled immigration. “Ever since I’ve been in high school, I’ve seen how things are with some people who immigrate and don’t want to integrate,” he said.

At a demonstration elsewhere in Orléans on Saturday, left-wing critics of the far-right party said the opposite. “We are all children of immigrants,” read a protester’s sign. Many expressed outrage over Friday’s deadly shooting in the Paris suburb, Trappes, and a neighboring village, La Verrière. Though the details of what happened remain incomplete, critics claimed the violence had reflected the nativist language and anti-immigrant policies of the National Rally.

“The reality is that we are witnessing the normalization of far-right rhetoric here,” said Olivier Faure, the head of the Socialist Party. “If the far right were to win next year, it would usher in a state-sponsored xenophobic policy.”

Ali Rabeh, the left-wing mayor of Trappes, who also marched, said the shooting had whipped up “fear and anxiety.” The death toll could have been higher, he said, citing intelligence that the assailant had planned to target two mosques.

“One wonders whether, simply due to the color of one’s skin, one might be targeted on a street corner while out buying a baguette or visiting family,” Mr. Rabeh said.

item.title: Here’s What to Know About Brazil’s Election
item.description:
Brazilians head to the polls Sunday to elect a new president in a fiercely fought election that is the biggest test yet for an ascendant right winning presidencies across Latin America.

The contest also carries major consequences for U.S. ambitions for political and economic dominance in the region, pitting a leftist incumbent who has repeatedly defied President Trump against a right-wing rival aligned with Washington on issues like using lethal force to fight drug gangs.

Voters will decide whether to give President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva another term or elect Flávio Bolsonaro, a senator and the son of the last president.

Mr. Bolsonaro heads into the race as the front-runner, having won more ballots than Mr. Lula in the first round of voting this month but not enough to avoid a runoff. Still, the margin was the smallest in Brazil’s history and most polls show the two men in essentially a statistical tie.

The two candidates offer starkly different visions for the future of Latin America’s largest democracy on issues that include how to fight organized crime, shake up a sluggish economy and restore trust in Brazil’s institutions.

The presidential contest is a familiar one, pitting Mr. Lula, once again, against a Bolsonaro. This time, though, he will face off against the eldest son of the former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom Mr. Lula defeated in 2022.

Mr. Bolsonaro was convicted last year on charges of orchestrating a vast coup plot, which included plans to assassinate Mr. Lula.

Mr. Lula, 80, has framed his candidacy as a vote for democracy and the only way to bar the return of the Bolsonaro family to power. His argument has struck a chord with Brazilians worried about the health of Brazil’s democracy if another Bolsonaro leads the country.

Mr. Lula has also promised to protect Brazil’s sovereignty, standing up to Mr. Trump last year when he tried, through tariffs and sanctions, to help Jair Bolsonaro avoid prison.

Yet Mr. Lula, an enduring presence in Brazilian politics who is now seeking a fourth term, has also struggled to energize many voters hungry for political and economic change. The first round of voting suggested that he has lost touch with many working-class Brazilians who were once his staunchest backers.

Mr. Bolsonaro, 45, seeking to harness the affection many right-wing voters still have for Jair Bolsonaro, has promised to restore his father conservative agenda. At the same time, he is trying to appeal to women and independent voters by casting himself as a more moderate successor by avoiding the sexist, racist and homophobic rhetoric that his father often employed.

Mr. Bolsonaro has said that, if elected, he would seek amnesty for his father and rioters jailed for storming Brazil’s halls of power after the last election, in an episode reminiscent of the attack on the U.S. Capitol.

Each candidate has cast the other as corrupt. Mr. Lula has pointed to a corruption investigation into Mr. Bolsonaro over millions of dollars he raised for a biopic about his father from a disgraced banker at the center of a billion-dollar fraud scandal. Mr. Bolsonaro has seized on a past corruption scandal that landed Mr. Lula in jail, a conviction that was later set aside.

Brazilian voters are seeking solutions to various challenges, including the spread of criminal networks and persistent economic stagnation that has left many people under financial strain.

Mr. Bolsonaro, seizing on voter worries about crime, has made fighting drug gangs a cornerstone of his campaign. He has vowed to “declare war” on crime groups and build five new maximum-security prisons inspired by the incarceration model adopted by El Salvador’s strongman, Nayib Bukele.

Mr. Lula has championed a different approach that targets the finances and weapons of organized criminal organizations, arguing that these groups must be dismantled from the top. He has pointed to Brazil’s history of bloody police operations that take out foot soldiers but fail to capture gang leaders.

Mr. Bolsonaro, inspired by President Javier Milei of Argentina, has adopted a pair of giant scissors as a symbol of a leaner state and promised $40 billion in cuts to public spending. He has also pledged to lower taxes and reduce red tape for entrepreneurs, seeking to appeal to a growing number of Brazilian workers who have migrated to the gig economy.

Under Mr. Lula’s watch, Brazil’s economy has remained largely unscathed by American tariffs while unemployment rates have dropped to record lows. Still, rising food prices and mounting household debt have weighed on his approval ratings.

Mr. Lula, seeking to reverse his fortunes, recently expanded a debt-relief program under which the government will buy billions in delinquent consumer loans. And just days before the elections, he banned online betting, which has accelerated Brazil’s personal debt crisis.

In Brazil, a nation where protecting its sovereignty runs deep, worries about America putting its thumb on the vote has loomed large.

Mr. Lula, casting Mr. Bolsonaro as a U.S. puppet, has accused the Trump administration of trying to sway the vote in his rival’s favor to seize Brazil’s vast natural resources, including critical minerals.

He has also frequently reminded voters that Mr. Trump applied steep tariffs on Brazil after a brother of Flávio Bolsonaro lobbied the White House as part of a campaign to keep their father out of prison. When those efforts failed, Mr. Trump dropped most of those tariffs.

While Mr. Trump has not formally endorsed the younger Mr. Bolsonaro, he has seemed willing to support him in more subtle ways. This has included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist organizations, which helped Mr. Bolsonaro cast Mr. Lula as weak on crime.

Following Mr. Bolsonaro’s first-round win, Mr. Trump was quick to celebrate. “It’s a big victory,” he told reporters.

In recent days, questions have also emerged over the impartiality of American social media companies after Mr. Lula and independent watchdog groups accused Meta of giving his right-wing rival favorable treatment on its platforms.

In the race to sway a deeply divided Brazil, social media has emerged as a contentious political battleground since the first round of voting. And Brazil’s electoral court has become the referee that some accuse of picking sides.

The court, led by a justice appointed by Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, has ordered social media posts by news outlets criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed and barred Mr. Lula from posting some negative news stories about his rival.

Justice Kássio Nunes Marques, who leads the electoral court, set off widespread outrage by appearing to target a popular channel on WhatsApp, a platform long dominated by Mr. Bolsonaro’s right-wing movement, aimed at mobilizing Mr. Lula’s supporters on social media and on the streets.

The channel, which quickly attracted more 10 million followers, landed in the center of a firestorm when Mr. Bolsonaro asked the electoral court to shut it down, claiming it was spreading fake news.

Ultimately, the channel was allowed to keep operating, though Justice Nunes Marques pressed Meta to dig deeper to see if it was breaking any electoral rules.

On Sunday, Brazilians will cast their votes using electronic voting machines; experts say it is one of the fastest and most secure electoral systems in the world. Voting in Brazil is compulsory and, in 2022, turnout for the second round of elections was close to 80 percent.

Brazil’s electoral authority will start releasing results after polls close at 4 p.m. E.T., and a final tally will most likely be announced a few hours later. The count can be followed in real time here.

item.title: María Corina Machado, Venezuela’s Leading Opposition Figure, Returns Home
item.description:
Venezuela’s most popular opposition leader, María Corina Machado, has returned to her country after nearly a year in exile, according to a spokesman.

The spokesman, David Smolansky, in a statement, called the return “a major step toward a democratic transition and free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections in the near future.”

Ms. Machado’s efforts to return to Venezuela have been fraught with political tension in recent months. The former member of Venezuela’s Legislature has led the opposition for the past three years, spending much of that time living in hiding inside her country, trying to avoid arrest.

She fled last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Then, after the United States captured Venezuela’s autocrat, Nicolás Maduro, in January in a raid on Caracas, the Trump administration chose to elevate another member of his repressive government, Delcy Rodríguez, to the presidency.

Tensions between the Trump administration and Ms. Machado have been high since.

Ms. Machado has repeatedly promised to return to her country and push for elections, telling The New York Times in a recent interview that her homecoming would arrive “sooner than you would expect.”

In a message on X at 11:31 a.m. Venezuela time, Ms. Machado wrote: “I am here. With you all.”

Her party also shared images of her in a church in Lara State, in the western part of the country, indicating that the photographs confirmed her arrival in Venezuela.

On Sunday after her announcement, President Trump told reporters in Washington: “She’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe, she’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing really well in Venezuela.”

Mr. Smolansky, the aide to Ms. Machado, wrote in his statement: “We thank President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the U.S. Government, Congress, and allied governments for their continued leadership and support.”

“Ms. Machado returns to stand with Venezuelans in their pursuit of freedom, democracy, and justice,” he added, “and to help advance a peaceful, inclusive, and sustainable transition leading to free, fair, and verifiable presidential elections, with guarantees for all.”

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
